title: Flowing (Taking Notes)
summary: Debaters take notes in columns, one per speech, so every argument and its answers line up across the page. A good flow shows you what was answered, what was dropped, and what to say next.

p: A **flow** is a sheet of notes with one column for each speech. You write each argument in the column of the speech where it was made, and write the answers to it in the next column, on the same line. Reading across a row shows the life of one argument through the round; that's why it's called a flow.
Many debaters use two sheets: one for the affirmative case and one for the negative case, so answers line up next to what they answer.
*Resolved: In a democracy, voting ought to be compulsory.* Lincoln-Douglas, affirmative case sheet. Each column is one speech; arrows (→) mean "answers."

rows: → Prefer liberty / autonomy: dem exists to protect choice
→ Autonomy needs a voice; low turnout = unequal voice
→ Even under autonomy: can vote blank, choice kept
C1: Low turnout skews who's heard (turnout gaps by age, income)
→ Gaps shrink w/ easier registration (no force needed)
→ Easier reg tried; gaps remain (ev: same states)
→ Alts help but don't close gap; only full turnout does
→ Turn: duty to vote → people pay attention
→ Dropped turn: extend: more engaged voters
Off: Liberty violation: fines punish non-voters
→ Small fine, exemptions, blank ballot OK
→ Weigh: tiny burden vs. whole nation's voice
flow.note: Made-up round for practice. Abbreviations: V = value, C = criterion, C1 = contention one, Ext = extend, ↑ = increases, ↓ = decreases, ev = evidence, w/ = with, ≠ = is not.

list: **Use abbreviations and symbols.** ↑ up, ↓ down, → leads to or answers, ∴ therefore, ≠ not, $ money, w/ with, b/c because. Make up your own for each topic.
**Write taglines, not sentences.** "C1: turnout skews who's heard" is enough.
**Leave room.** Space the first speech's arguments out so the answers fit beside them.
**Use two colors** (one per side) if it helps you see who said what.
**Flow the cross-ex admissions** in a margin, so you can use them in your speech.
**Mark drops.** Circle or star arguments the other side didn't answer.

sections.h: Using your flow in a speech
p: Before each speech, look across your flow. Every argument against you should have an answer in your column; every argument of yours they didn't answer is a drop to extend. Then give your speech in the order of the flow, signposting each line ("On their first contention..."), so the judge can follow along on their own flow.

Experienced judges (often called **flow judges**) keep their own flow and decide the round from it. Clear signposting and taglines make it easy for them to write your arguments in the right place. Parent and community judges may take simpler notes; help them by summarizing clearly. See [Judging and Ballots](/debate/learn/judging-and-ballots/).

practice: Flow a recorded debate (one of the national finals in [Resources](/debate/resources/)) on paper or with the on-screen flow sheet.
Have a partner read a one-minute speech with three arguments; flow it, then answer each one in the next column.
Make a list of ten abbreviations for your current topic.
